XXVIII QUESTIONS ABOUT THE HEPTATEUCH
REASON AND DATE OF COMPOSITION OF THE “QUAESTIONES IN HEPTATEUCHUM”

The reason why Augustine composed this work is clearly explained by the author in the prologue: «When I read the so-called canonical Holy Scriptures with a certain speed and compared the translations with those of other codices, made on the version of the Septuagint, it seemed useful to me to collect in a writing some questions that came to my mind so that I would not forget them, whether it was a matter of briefly remembering them, or just of proposing them, even with some detail, or of solving them in some way, even if it was very quickly. It was not about explaining them exhaustively, but about being able to take a look when I needed to do so, or to check what I still had to investigate, or to be ready not only to think, but also prepared to respond, according to my possibilities, based on what seemed to me to have already been sufficiently investigated. The work does not belong, therefore, to the literary genre of the Commentarii, but of the Quaestiones, widely used before and after Saint Augustine, and which the author himself used in at least eight of his works 2, and which consisted of explanations, generally brief, sometimes very brief, of specific biblical passages that I will make the quotations from the Quaestiones in Heptateuchum in Spanish, according to my translation, referring to vol. XXVIII, Pars II, from the CSEL, Vindobonae (Vienna) 1895 (Introduction), p.3. I will make the other citations of the works of Saint Augustine sometimes in PL, by Migne, vol. XXXII-XLVI, and others, by the Corpus Christianorum (CC). Augustine says this same thing in Retract. 2.55: PL 32,651-652: «Eodem tempore scripsi etiam libros Quaestionum de libris eisdem divinis septem, quod ideo appellare sic volui, quia ea quae ibi disputantur, magis quaerenda proposui, quam quaesita dissolvi; quamvis multo plura in eis mihi videantur ita pertractata, ut possint etiam soluta et expósita non immerito iudicari». The author of Quaestiones thus had at hand in a volume the explanation he needed in a given case, either because someone asked him a question, or because the author himself used it in some controversial work, or even because he needed it for a sermon or a preaching. The very fact of already posing a problem, even if the solution is not found at the moment, is already a beginning of research, and, therefore, something useful: "Because - as Agustín says - part of research consists of knowing what one should investigate" 3. LITERARY GENRE OF «QUAESTIONES»
In patristic literature before Augustine

The literary genre of the Quaestiones occupied a prominent place in antiquity, starting in the Alexandrian period. Despite the different names it received, it was always the same genre, that is, problems related to a text that one was trying to solve, or difficulties that had to be explained, or doubts that had to be clarified. Sacred Scripture, like philosophy, offered an appropriate field for the development of this genre. With respect to the Commentaries themselves, the Questions offered the advantage of not claiming a special style, leaving the author complete freedom to lengthen or shorten the exposition. Not even a minimum of introduction to the matter was needed. You could enter directly into the topic—in medias res, as the Latins would say—without detours, and you could develop the topic or answer the problem in one line, in several lines, or in several pages. Augustine, as we will see, offers examples of all these data 26. b)

These eight works, as Bardy 27 says, are very different from each other, both in their importance and in their content. Some are very brief; others, quite spacious. The broad ones contain a systematic repertoire of the problems posed by a book or a group of books. The briefs solve a certain number of problems in no special order. Some of these books are addressed to specific people who corresponded with Augustine. Others, the majority, are aimed at the general public. The Questions on the Heptateuch respond to real problems that Augustine faced in reading and explaining the books of Scripture. But Augustine also exposes and clarifies issues resolved by others. In any case, the literary genre of the Questions represents a selection of themes or scholia. And it is not a commentary following a biblical book or the entire Holy Scripture. c)
The "Quaestiones" of Jerome and Augustine on Genesis

Augustine's work on the Heptateuch begins in Gen 4:17 [Cain, founder of a city]. The omission of the first three chapters of Genesis, so important in biblical revelation, requires a brief explanation, which Augustine himself offers us in the prologue to the Quaestiones: «Thus, Cf. G. BARDY, l.c, p.515.

Leaving aside those points from the beginning, when it is said that God made heaven and earth, until the expulsion of the first parents from paradise, matters that can be treated in many ways, and which I have already dealt with elsewhere according to my possibilities, here are the themes that I wanted to put in writing, as they presented themselves to me as I read them. until Gen 3:24; the De Genesi ad litteram, written from 401, and which reaches Gen 3:23. But on Genesis, in addition to the works reviewed, he dealt not only with the Quaestiones in Genesim and the Locutions in Genesim, written at the same time, as I have said, 29, but also with books Abel until the flood; and book X V I (in 43 chapters), the sacred history, from Noah and the flood to the entry of the Israelites into Egypt (end of Genesis and beginning of the Exodus). And, finally, there are also numerous quotes from Genesis in the books Contra Adimantum, a work written in the year 394, and in the Contra Faustum manichaeum, written in the year 400. Saint Augustine, therefore, dealt very extensively with Genesis, and his name appears, or should always appear, among the commentators on Genesis. Augustine uses, when the occasion requires it, the solutions approved by other commentators before him. For Genesis he used the Quaestiones hebraicae in Genesim, by Jerome 31. For the other books of the Heptateuch he used other sources, as I will expressly say in the explanatory notes. Among these we can now mention Saint Ambrose, whose works De Abraham libri duo, De Isaac et anima, De Ioseph patriarcha and others, which deal with the same themes of Augustine's Questions, the Doctor of Hippo made use of, using above all many allegorical interpretations of Saint Ambrose 32.

As regards Genesis, it is curious that, of the 220 Questions that Jerome dedicates to it, and of the 173 that Augustine dedicates to it, only 30 themes coincide 35. And to clarify these same themes, The positions of Jerome and Augustine are almost always different, if not contrary, according to the method and particular concerns of each one. They disagree, first of all, about the text that should serve as a basis for the explanation. Jerome seeks, above all, the Hebraic sales, the accuracy of the Greek version of the Septuagint in relation to the Hebrew text, pointing out translation errors, additions, deletions and other possible errors in any version. Augustine, on the other hand, bases his explanation on a Latin version made about the Septuagint, and never attempts to correct them, but rather to explain them. Augustine will rarely add texts foreign to the Seventy to support his explanations. If you go to manuscripts, it is always to compare them with the Greek text of the Septuagint and to see which ones are most in line with them. The Greek versions of Aquila and Symmachus only serve to confirm or clarify the version of the Seventy. The absolute authority of the Seventy was for Augustine an unquestionable truth, and he maintains this in many places, such as in the De civ. There is, therefore, no greater discrepancy between Jerome and Augustine regarding the text that had to be used for the commentary: the Hebrew text, according to Jerome; the Greek text of the Septuagint, according to Augustine. Let us now look at some specific cases in which they also differ in the explanation of the Questions of Genesis that are common to them. In Gen 47:31 the gesture made by Jacob when his son Joseph took an oath is described. Jerome solves the problem by saying: "And Israel bowed down at the head of the bed," a gesture that, according to him, would indicate the gored posture he adopted when praying. Augustine, on the other hand, following the Septuagint, whose Latin version says: "And Israel bowed down on the end of his staff," recognizes that the solution "in the Hebrew text is very easy," but that does not mean that we should think that what the Septuagint says makes no sense or has very little sense."42 Regarding the age of Methuselah (Gen 5:26-28), who, according to the chronology of the Seventy, would have lived fourteen years after the flood, whereas Scripture says that in the flood all men perished except those who had entered the ark with Noah, Jerome, in his commentary, admits that there is an error in the figures, and alludes to the Hebrew and Samaritan text, in which the date of the death of Methuselah coincides with the year of the beginning of the flood. THE BIBLICAL TEXT OF THE «QUAESTIONES»

Augustine refers many times in the Quaestiones to other translations and other translators 61. With regard to the codices, Augustine sometimes speaks, in general, of multi; plerique; nonnulli; aliqui; there codices; and others, specifically, multi latini; Latin quidam latini; nonnulli latini codices; latini codices plurimi; latini codices paene omnes. The author also talks about graeci codices; graece scriptum est; graeci; graecus or graeca exemplaria. The translators also mention them, or in general, with the following expressions: aliqui; quidam alii interpreters; quidam interpreters, or, specifically, latini; aliqui; quidam latini interpreters. He also speaks of nostri interpreters; nonnulli interpretes nostri; Quidam nostri interpretes. The number of codices that Augustine used for his Quaestiones was not small. In one case he used six manuscripts: one Latin; another Greek; a third Greek and three more: one Greek, and two Latin 62. Other times he talks about better and worse codices 63 and the defects of some codices 64. When Augustine cites the Greek (Graecus) without further explanation, he always refers to the version of the Septuagint, and precisely to the recension transmitted by the Alexandrian codex (= A). When he cites the Graecus in Latin, which is normal and most frequent, he refers to the literal version, known as Itala, which Augustine himself says elsewhere is verborum tenacior cum perspicuitate sententiae65. The entire work of textual criticism for Augustine consisted of choosing a good Latin version, among the many that were then circulating, and correcting any variants it had in relation to the Greek text. The Latin version that he liked the most was, as I just said, the Italian, since it met the two fundamental conditions for him: the Latin words were well intelligible and the Greek text was transparent in them. Rüting distinguishes three groups of Questions, which Augustine himself hints at in the introduction to his work: 1) The first group includes questions that only consist of questions and do not receive a solution. They are usually introduced with the formulas: Quid est? Quod sití Quid sibi vultí Quaeritur. Quaeri solet. Quaestio est. VALUE OF THE EXEGESIS OF ST. AUGUSTINE

Many of Saint Augustine's exegetical solutions, as we will have the opportunity to see in the explanatory notes to the translation, surprise us today for their naivety and lack of historical perspective to place the biblical books and scriptural events in their corresponding framework. In this sense it is evident that Agustín has lacked the necessary knowledge, since the picture of his historical and chronological knowledge is very limited, although it must be recognized, in his defense, that in most cases it could not be otherwise. We are sometimes surprised by their ingenuity in defending the literal meaning of many biblical passages, to explain which it would have been enough to admit the fact, fundamentally historical, and leave all the other details as mere literary garb, whose historicity does not need to be admitted. Thus, for example, Augustine defends without the slightest hesitation the longevity of the first men, without realizing that it could be some hidden symbolism of numbers or some religious nuance that would have to be investigated. Noah's Ark gives him the opportunity to exercise his ingenuity, first, to defend its historicity, even in the smallest details, and then to make beautiful disquisitions on allegories of future events. Examples of this type could be multiplied indefinitely; but we leave them for the explanatory notes of the translation 87. Augustine, as a man of his time, conditioned by the culture of his time, could not in many cases give another solution than the one he gave. But in his defense it must be said that he used figures of speech more than other writers of his time to explain the message of the Bible. But we must not forget the allegorical sense either. In the Quaestioms there is a certain balance between literal meaning and allegorical meaning. Simple explanations should serve the Christian faithful with little theological or doctrinal training in order to be able to face many objections from the enemies of the faith. Augustine does not expressly deal in the Quaestiones with the inspiration of Holy Scripture, since this truth is for him something evident that does not need demonstration, nor does he propose it in this work. And in another place he adds: "Therefore, a serious question arises of knowing how those tables that Moses was going to break, knowing that God beforehand, it is said that they were not the work of man, but of God, and that they had not been written by man, but by God, by the finger of God" 93. Results and value of Augustinian exegesis

It refers to the relationship between the Old and New Testaments, since both are vehicles of the same divine revelation. According to Augustine, the New Testament is hidden in the Old, and the Old is manifested in the New. The Augustinian formulation of this truth has become classic. We find it repeated, almost always with the same words, in q.2,73: Quamquam et in vetere novum lateat et in novo vetus patat. This hermeneutical principle has important consequences for the exegesis, especially allegorical, of Scripture, and Augustine has not failed to underline it many times in the Quaestiones™. Regarding the author of the Pentateuch, Augustine has ideas that do not differ too much from ours in terms of the substance of the problem, although they differ greatly in the details. Of course, and first of all, it affirms that Moses is the author of the Pentateuch. This is what he presupposes when he quotes the phrase from Scripture that says: "that Moses was adorned with all the wisdom of the Egyptians" 101. And he expressly states it when he says: "But of all these (kings of Edom) Moses could only mention those who existed before his death" ~iT<y. However, in the Quaestiones there is sufficient data to deduce that this opinion of Augustine was much more nuanced and the Holy Doctor had his doubts about the Mosaic authorship of the entire Pentateuch in its current form. Thus, Augustine sometimes speaks simply of the writer or narrator of the Pentateuch, without expressly mentioning Moses 103. And Augustine recognizes that in the Pentateuch there is an editorial work, according to which the historical order of events is not always respected. Commenting on the text of Num 16:36-38, he says: «Scripture had already recalled this in the Exodus, when describing the construction of the altar. Therefore, it is understood that the different events were distributed by books, not according to the exact order of time" 104. OUR SPANISH VERSION OF THE «QUAESTIONES»

The Spanish version that I offer of this dense, erudite and not easy work by the Bishop of Hippo has sought more fidelity to the thought than the literality of the expression, although, in reality, I have tried to stay in the middle, seeking balance. It is not easy to translate Saint Augustine. His endless periods, full of subordinate clauses, betray, even after so many years—more than forty-five years after the beginning of his profession as a rhetorician—they betray, I say, the professor of rhetoric. I have systematically tried to shorten the periods, to bring Augustine's bombastic and rhetorical language closer to our language and current use. This, with regard to Augustine's text, his explanations and disquisitions. As regards the biblical text, however, I have sought the greatest possible literality, following the Latin text of the Augustinian Bible, which was an ancient Latin version, the famous and still unidentified Italian, much more vulgar and less elegant than Jerome's Vulgate. And I have done so, often at the risk of offering a clearly obscure meaning and difficult language, so that the explanation that Augustine gives in his Quaestiones may later have some meaning. Because, if I had translated many biblical texts more freely, or simply based on the Vulgate, many of the difficulties that Augustine explains would have disappeared. The translation of the Bible, therefore, necessarily had to be literal. The abundant notes collect, first of all, all the biblical quotations related to the text that Augustine comments on. I. the Scripture that Tharra, Abram's father, begat Abram when he was seventy years old and then remained with all his people in Harran and lived two hundred and five years in Harran and died, and that the Lord commanded Abram to leave Harran and he left there, Abraham being seventy-five years old? 33 The answer would be that the Scripture says by way of recapitulation that the Lord spoke while Tarra was still alive and that, while his father was still alive, Abram left Harran, according to the commandment of the Lord, at the age of seventy-five years, when his father was one hundred and forty-five, if the years of his father's life were two hundred and five, so that it is written that the years of the life of Tharra were two hundred and five in Harran, because there he fulfilled all the years of his entire life. The question, therefore, is resolved by resorting to recapitulation, since it would remain unresolved if we considered that after the death of Tharra the Lord commanded Abram to leave Harran, because he could not have been only seventy-five years old when his father died, who fathered him at the age of seventy, so that Abram would be one hundred and thirty years old, after the death of his father, if all that he lived were two hundred and five. In short, if this type of recapitulation used by Scripture is taken into account, many problems that otherwise seem

soluble, as we have said above regarding other questions, which we have also resolved by turning to it 34. However, there are others 35 that solve the problem in a different way, saying that the years of Abram's life are computed from the moment in which he was freed from the fire or the Chaldeans, in which they accused him of having wanted to worship him according to their superstition. And although Scripture does not say that he was freed from that fire, Jewish tradition remembers it. The problem can also be solved in the following way: The text that says: When Tharra was seventy-five years old he begat Abram, Nahor and Haran, evidently does not mean that he begat the three at the age of seventy years, but that the Scripture remembers the year from which he began to have children. But it may be that Abram was begotten later, and because of his excellence, for which he is frequently praised in Scripture, he was mentioned before, just as the prophet first mentioned the younger: I loved Jacob and hated Esau. And in the book of Paralipomena, Judas is mentioned first, despite occupying fourth place in the order of birth, because he is the one who gives the name to the Jewish lineage because his tribe is the royal tribe. In short, different solutions are quite easily found to solve difficult questions.

The explanation that Saint Augustine gives of Jacob's struggle with the angel (= with God) (Gen 32,23-33) is allegorical and mystical. The real explanation is to see here an ancient tradition to explain the name Penuel (= "Face of God") and clarify the origin of the name Israel. In the midst of the combat, when Jacob discovers that he is fighting with a supernatural being, whose name he does not want to tell him, he forces him to give him the blessing so that this blessing will then pass to all those who will later bear the name of Jacob-Israel. This scene has been interpreted by some Holy Fathers as an image of spiritual combat and a symbol of the effectiveness of persevering prayer.

But this solution to the problem must be confirmed with some example of another similar expression. There is no easier solution to this question than to resort to a synecdoche. Thus, when a part in a whole is larger or more important, what does not belong to the name itself is usually also designated by its name. For example, the case of Judas, who no longer belonged to the twelve apostles, because he had already died when the Lord rose from the dead, and yet the Apostle maintains the number of twelve in his letter, when he says that the Lord appeared to the twelve. The Greek codices have this word with an article, in such a way that not any twelve people can be understood, but only those known by that number. In the story of the "plagues" there are several traditions, although it is difficult to separate in detail what corresponds to each one. The "priestly" tradition presents Aaron next to Moses. The miracles that Aaron performs with the help of his staff accredit Moses as God's representative. The "Yahwist" tradition presents Moses intervening alone before the Pharaoh, and Yahweh himself begins and ends the announced plague. It is more difficult to separate the "Elohist" tradition. The passages in which Moses performs miracles, whether or not he has in his hand the “staff—rod—of God,” probably belong to it. It is God himself who gives Moses his staff (or rod) (cf. Ex 4:17.20; 7:20b; 9:22ff; 10:13ff, etc.). In short: Aaron has his staff (or rod) like Moses has his staff (or rod), according to the different traditions.

There were too many men to cross the Red Sea with their livestock in one night (Ex 14:22-27), and, on the other hand, the text says that they could not occupy Canaan because they were few (Ex 23:29.30). The figure, therefore, does not seem to have mathematical value.

It may be a historical idealization to highlight the fulfillment of the great descendants of Abraham; That is to say, that number seems to obey religious reasons and not historical or mathematical reasons. Augustine develops an allegorical interpretation here, when the reality is simpler: The slaves received a tattoo on their wrist and face, so that if they fled, they would be recognized. Worshipers of a god could do the same (cf. Ezek 9:4-6). Yahweh commands that the Israelites do it as a perpetual and faithful remembrance. It was to be a sign and reminder of the observance of the law.

The question is also often raised whether the word moechia (adultery) also includes fornication 50. Moechia is a Greek word that Scripture already uses in Latin. But in Greek only adulterers are called moechios. Naturally, this law has not only been given for men, but also for women. In fact, because the Scripture says: You shall not desire your neighbor's wife, the woman should not think that nothing is prohibited here, and therefore that she can lawfully desire her neighbor's husband. Therefore, if from what is said here to the man it follows that the precept also includes the woman, although it is not expressly said, how much more must the precept on the prohibition of adultery refer to both sexes, when the precept itself can refer without difficulty to both; the same as the commandments: Thou shalt not kill; you shall not steal, and any similar ones that did not expressly refer to one sex, would apply to both sexes equally. But when only one gender is expressed, then the noblest gender is expressed, that is, the masculine gender, so that through it the woman also understands what is commanded. Obviously, a married man who has sexual relations with a woman who is not his wife is also an adulterer, even if she is not married. But the problem rightly arises of knowing whether those who have these relationships without being married, be it the man or the woman, violate this precept. Because if they do not break it, then fornication would not be prohibited in the Decalogue. Only moechia would be, that is, adultery, although all moechia is understood to also be fornication, as the Scriptures say. For the Lord says in the Gospel: Everyone who divorces his wife, except in the case of fornication, causes her to commit adultery. Here the sexual relationship between a married woman with a man other than her husband is called fornication, an act that is a moechia, that is, adultery. Therefore, in the Scriptures, all moechia is also fornication. But that all fornication can also be a moechia, I cannot find any example that supports it in the Scriptures at the moment. Now, if not all fornication can also be moechia, I do not know in what precept of the Decalogue that fornication that unmarried men commit with unmarried women can be prohibited. It does not belong to the sense of sight, but to hearing. But, just as I just said videatur (seems), applying this word to all the things I said, so videre (see) is usually used in a general sense, not only to refer to corporeal things, but also to spiritual things. Some believe that "seeing" the voice means nothing more than "understanding", an act that is the vision of the mind. Well, since here the author briefly wanted to say that the people saw the voice and the lightning and the sound of the trumpet and the mountain emitting smoke, an even greater problem would arise if we wanted to know what the lightning and the mountain emitting smoke were heard, things that belong to the sense of sight. The problem is solved by saying that the author did not have to have said it so briefly to be able to cover everything: he heard the voice and saw the lightning and heard the sound of the trumpet and saw the mountain smoking. There were, therefore, two kinds of voices: those coming from the clouds, like thunder, and those coming from the trumpet, if the sound that came from the clouds is actually called a voice. And so, in things referring to the sense of hearing, the author refers to the general sense, that is, that of sight, the Scripture wanting to briefly cover the whole, rather than in things that refer to the sense of sight the sense of hearing would have been understood, since we do not usually speak that way. When one kills voluntarily, he kills and God delivers it into his hands. There is, then, this difference, that in that case, only God has done it; In this case, however, God and man do it by the will of the one who does it. But man does not do it like God. 107 (Ex 26,1). Scripture commands that the tabernacle be made with ten tapestries, since it is the decalogue of the law. The tapestries mean the width in attention to the ease. Charity is the fullness of the law and only the precepts of charity are easy. Therefore the same width is recommended, when it is said: You have enlarged my steps under me and my steps have not become weak. But since this enlargement is done by the grace of God—for the love of God has been poured into our hearts, not by ourselves, but by the Holy Spirit given to us—therefore this same number is mystically recommended here, which also refers to the Holy Spirit, through whom the law can be fulfilled. It is said that the tapestry must be twenty-eight cubits in length. Well, this same number, since it must be divided by seven, means that the width of the tapestry must be four cubits. Because four times seven is twenty-eight. And this is also a perfect number, because, like six, it consists of its parts. And what Scripture says so many times: You will embroider cherubs on it, what else does it reveal in all those places but the abundance of knowledge, which the word cherub means?*2.

107 (Ex 26,1). Decem aulaeorum iubetfieri tabernaculum, cum sit decalogus legis. Aulaea uero significant latitudinem propter facilitatem. In this phrase the narrator's mode changes, and like someone who predicts and preannounces something, he begins to pronounce the words of the future tense. For it does not say: At the command of the Lord the children of Israel "placed" the camp, but they will place it. Nor does it say: At the command of the Lord "they rose up", but they will rise. And he preserves this same idiom also in what follows, an idiom very little used in the Scriptures. Because we know that future things have been predicted many times with words of past tense, for example: My hands and my feet have been pierced; and: he was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and many other examples. But it is very difficult to find in the Scriptures that the narrator of things past uses words of future tense. The Ammonite and the Moabite will not enter the assembly of the Lord; They will not enter the assembly of the Lord until the tenth generation or ever. The problem lies in how Ruth, who was a Moabite, entered, from whom the Lord even comes naturally. Perhaps we have to understand that it has been mystically prophesied that it would enter, as the text says: until the tenth generation. Because the generations are computed from Abraham, when Lot also lived, who begat the Moabites and the Ammonites by his own daughters, and it is discovered that, counting Abraham himself, there are ten generations until Solomon, who begat Boaz, second husband of Ruth. The generations are these: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, Phares, Esrom, Aram, Aminadab, Naasón, Salmon. Salmon begat Boaz, who married Ruth, who was a widow. Therefore it is seen that after the tenth generation he left descendants in the assembly of the Lord, giving sons to Boaz. But we can still rightly ask why it is added: nor ever. Perhaps because after the prophecy was fulfilled with this tenth generation, no other person from the Ammonites and Moabites entered the assembly of the Hebrew people? Or were these words rather said: not until the tenth generation, to mean, through a certain universality of the number ten, that they would never enter, in such a way that the author lived

would say this same thing, adding the following words: nor ever} And if this is true, then it seems that Ruth was admitted against this prohibition. Or was it forbidden to admit Ammonites and not Ammonite women, that is, men and not women? This solution would be understood above all because, when the Israelites defeated those people, they received the order to kill all the men and not the women, except those who had had sexual relations with men, since these women had dragged the people into fornication. But they wanted to spare the lives of the virgins, not imputing to them the guilt for which those people deserved defeat. And these people are also remembered here, as if wondering why the Lord would not have wanted to admit the Moabites and the Ammonites into the assembly of the Lord. To explain it, it is added: Because they did not come to meet you with bread and water when you were a catnin at the exit from Egypt, and because they brought Balaam, son of Beor, from Mesopotamia, against you to curse you. These faults, not even then, when that people was defeated, were attributed to the women, whom they preferred to keep alive.

Augustine's assumption that the Israelites took wine with them when they left Egypt is gratuitous. The entire long disquisition that follows is due to a bad punctuation of Augustine's Latin text, and, therefore, once the correct punctuation is made, the difficulty disappears. The original text does not say: “they sinned not for him”, but: “they sinned. Not for him", that is, "they are not for him": they are not his children - with a defect. Modern translators present translations like these: "Those whom he begot without fault sinned against him, a perverse and crooked generation." Another: "Those who are not his children have sinned against him—they are his stain—a perverse and devious generation." Jerome's Vulgate also goes along this same line. It goes like this: Veccaverunt ei, et non plii eius in sordibus: Generatío prava atque perversa. From all these versions, what is clear is that it should not be translated "they sinned not for him." The phrase: "those whom he begat without blemish" refers to the fact that the people of Israel, creation and workmanship of God, were a race without blemish, without sin; If he has sinned now, it is his fault, the fault of the people themselves. The phrase: “those who are not his children” means that the Israelites have behaved badly towards Yahweh; They have behaved with him as if they were not his children. "They are spiritually morons." In any case, Augustine's Latin translation is the one that did not understand the text. a]ei, PL.

The allegorical interpretation of Dt 33:1-5, given here by Augustine, has no basis in the text. It is, however, a rather obscure text, mainly because it is poorly preserved in the Hebrew original, and the version used by Augustine differs greatly from the original text. The fundamental ideas of the passage are the following: a) God liberated his people, taking them out of Egypt and appearing to them radiant and majestic on Sinai. b) God walks with his heavenly court—the angels—and with his people, whom he chose from among all the peoples of the earth, c) The people, gathered on Sinai, surrender to God to fulfill his will, d) The people of Israel become the inheritance of God, e) Yahweh is, therefore, the king of Israel, who reigns over the tribes solemnly gathered under their leaders. Augustine's text is often unintelligible.

After having commanded this to the people, Joshua sent spies to Jericho, because, after crossing the Jordan, it was the nearest city. They left to go to the house of the prostitute Rahab, who hid them. The king looked for them and did not find them. She let them escape through a window and advised them to hide for three days in the mountains. Four days may have been spent on all these events. Thus, after the spies reported how the situation was around them, Joshua began the morning march with all the people from the place where he was. When he reached the Jordan, he turned away and stayed there. The people receive another harangue to prepare to cross the Jordan after three days, carrying the ark of the Lord ahead. From this it is deduced that it was a human disposition through which the people were ordered to prepare provisions, as if they were going to cross the aforementioned river after three days. of animals. But since they had a meaning and were like shadows of things to come, God wanted to recommend to us the very things signified by these sacrifices. And furthermore this was a convenient reason for those sacrifices to be changed and not to be imposed now, even more so, to be prohibited from offering them, so that we would not think that God truly delighted in such sacrifices with a carnal affection. But we rightly ask ourselves whether it was also appropriate that future things should be indicated by human sacrifices, not so that with them we should be horrified and fear in this case the deaths of men, who in any case must sometimes die, if those who would welcome this being done to them were placed in the hands of God for an eternal reward. If this were true, this kind of sacrifice would not displease God. But Scripture itself testifies clearly enough that these sacrifices displease God. Because if, on the one hand, God wanted and commanded that all the firstborn were consecrated to him and that they were his; On the other hand, he wanted the firstborn of men to be rescued, so that the people would not believe that they had to sacrifice their first-born children to God. Furthermore, this is demonstrated even more clearly by the fact that God so disapproves of human sacrifices that he prohibits these same sacrifices, detesting them in other nations and ordering his people not to dare to imitate them. For the text says like this: But when the Lord your God gnificatiua fuerint et quaedam umbrae Futurum, res ipsas nobis quae his sacrificiis significantur commendare uoluisse; Fuisse autem etiam istam utilem causam cur illa mutarentur nec moda iuberentur, immo prohiberentur offerri, ne uere secundum carnalem adfectum talibus deum delectan putaremus. Sed utrum etiam humanis sacrificiis signify future oportuerit, merit quaeritur: non quo mortes hominum quandoque [482] moriturorum in hac causa exhorrescere et formidare debene(359)m\is, si illi, qui haec de se fieri gratanter acciperent, in aeternam remunerationem commendarentur deo. Be si hoc uerum esset, hoc genus sacrificerum deo non displiceret; displicere autem deo satis euidenter eadem scriptura testatur. But Jephthah did not make his daughter a burnt offering, like these, to the Lord, but he did it as it had been commanded that animal sacrifices should be made and it had been forbidden for men to be sacrificed. More similar to this seems to be the one that Abraham made, a sacrifice that the Lord ordered in a singular way to be offered to him, but without ordering with any general law that such sacrifices be sometimes made to him, but on the contrary, completely prohibiting them from being made. There is, then, a difference between what Jephthah did and what Abraham did, because Abraham offered his son under a command, while Jephthah did what was prohibited by the law and was not imposed by any special command. Furthermore, not only later in his law, but also then, God manifested in Abraham's own son that he did not delight in such sacrifices, since he forbade the father, whose faith he had tested by the command, to kill his son and placed at his disposal a ram to lawfully make the sacrifice, according to the custom of the ancients appropriate to those times. For he did not say, Whatever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me, I will offer as a burnt offering, but he said, Whoever comes out, I will offer. Without a doubt, with these words, he did not think of anything other than a human being. However, perhaps he did not think about his only daughter. Now, in such a glorious moment for her father, who could go to meet him before his daughter but perhaps his wife? In relation to the fact that I did not say whoever (in feminine), but whoever (in masculine) leaves the doors of my house, it must be said that Scripture usually uses the masculine for both genders; as, for example, referring to Abraham, the Scripture says: rising from the dead man, when the dead woman was his wife. The second testimony is found in the passage where these things related to the vow he made and its fulfillment are narrated. Well, before this event, the Scripture says: And the spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah, and went through Gilead and Manasseh and passed through the watchtower of Gilead, and from the watchtower of Gilead he passed to the children of Amman. Once achieved, he fulfilled what he had promised. But we must pay attention again to the fact that Gideon achieved salvation for the people, defeating and defeating the enemies with a great massacre, although not after making the ephod, but after having tempted the Lord, which, certainly, is a sin. The text reads like this: And Gideon said to the Lord, Let not your anger be angry against me; I will speak again and I will try again with the fleece. Gideon feared, in fact, the wrath of God, because he knew that he sinned by tempting God, something that God expressly prohibits in his law. And yet, this sin of his was followed by the evidence of an admirable miracle and the great prosperity of the victory and liberation of the people. Because God had already determined to come to the aid of his afflicted people and was using the spirit, not only honest and pious, but also defective and delinquent, of this leader, which he had taken to carry out this work and to predict what he wanted and fulfill what he had said. God granted many things to his people, not only through these who, although they sinned, are counted among the righteous, also through Saul, who was absolutely reprobate, because the spirit of God also came upon him and he prophesied, and not when he acted rightly, but when he was angry against David, a good and innocent man. Because the spirit of the Lord acts through the good and the evil, through uouerat et qua adepta quod uouerat soluit (cf. Jud 11,33.34). Rutsus enim consideradum est, quia Gideon, etsi non posteaquam fecit ephud, tamen posteaquam tentauit dominum, quod utique peccatum est, magna strage hostibus caesis atque superatis populo adquisiuit salutem; sic enim scriptum est: et dixit Gideon ad dominum: non irascatur indignatio tua in me; et loquar adhuc semel et tentabo adhuc semel in uellere (Jud 6:39). Iram quippe dei metuebat, quia nouerat se temptation peccare, quod deus in lege sua manifestissime prohibet (cf. Deut 6,16; Mt 4,7; Lk 4,12). Hoc tamen peccatum eius et mirabilis signi euidentia et magna uictoriae prosperitas liberationisque populi consecuta est. Although the devil and his angels can also be called a people of sadness quite conveniently, either because they achieve eternal misfortune for those they deceive, or because they themselves are destined for eternal misfortune. Jephthah responds to the elders of Gilead in the following way, a way that is certainly quite appropriate to express the prophecy much more clearly: Are you not the ones who hated me and expelled me from my father's house and drove me away from you? And why do you come now, when you are troubled? Something similar to this is prefigured in Joseph, despised by his brothers, who sold him.
